title: ‘Everyone Is Doing It’: The Truth About AI in Hollywood
gist: Puck founding partner and former entertainment lawyer Matt Belloni tells WIRED that AI use is already universal in Hollywood but socially stigmatized, and that the real driver is a cost squeeze: movie budgets keep rising while box office does not cover them, guilds will not concede labor costs, so savings must come from non-union below-the-line work and technology. He maps the resulting power shift — Netflix paying $587 million for Ben Affleck's AI company, Amazon's $50 billion OpenAI deal preceding it dumping a finished $40 million Sam Altman film, Amazon's MGM membership neutering the MPA's response to Sora — and argues the only remaining studio moat is verified authenticity, which is simultaneously being destroyed by paid astroturf marketing.

themes.theme: Adoption is universal, disclosure is not

insights.claim: AI use in Hollywood splits cleanly into corporate AI (process streamlining, search) where adoption is universal and uncontroversial, and generative AI for content creation where output quality remains detectably poor outside animation.
insights.speaker: Katie Drummond
insights.so_what: Model the two separately: back-office AI is already priced into studio opex, while generative content AI is still a call option whose strike is animation, not live action.
insights.locator: Well, there's two types of AI

insights.claim: Netflix disclosed on its earnings call that 300 shows use generative AI — the first major buyer to quantify adoption publicly and loudly rather than deny it.
insights.speaker: Katie Drummond
insights.so_what: A hard disclosure benchmark competitors will be measured against; watch whether Disney, WBD and Paramount follow with numbers or stay silent, which itself signals their exposure.
insights.quote: even Netflix, on their earnings call this past month, said that 300 shows use generative AI.
insights.locator: On the generative AI front

insights.claim: Creative-side AI use runs deeper than public statements suggest: a prominent showrunner reportedly castigated her writing team for NOT using ChatGPT in the creative process, and screenwriters use it for scenario and set-description generation.
insights.speaker: Katie Drummond
insights.so_what: Stated industry opposition to AI understates real adoption — do not use public creator sentiment as a proxy for enterprise software demand in media.
insights.locator: I'm not going to name a name

insights.claim: Social punishment for disclosed AI use is a live commercial risk: after Amazon's media day announcing shows from its generative AI studio run by Albert Chang, online backlash was loud enough that one attached creator stepped down.
insights.speaker: Katie Drummond
insights.so_what: AI shaming has demonstrated the ability to break attachments and delay projects — a real execution risk for studios marketing AI-assisted slates.
insights.quote: That's a tangible impact of AI shaming, so to speak, and that is real.
insights.locator: A perfect example is Amazon

insights.claim: Generative AI's first real disruption lands in animation, where scenes can be visually completed and storyboards produced without artists — not in live action, where the output is still detectable.
insights.speaker: Katie Drummond
insights.so_what: Concentrate both the upside (cost deflation) and the downside (job displacement) analysis on animation pipelines first; live-action VFX follows later.
insights.locator: I think where we're seeing the biggest innovation/disruption

themes.theme: Cost squeeze is the actual driver

insights.claim: The structural motive for studio AI adoption is a widening gap between rising production costs and box office that no longer covers them — cost reduction, not creative capability, is the C-suite priority.
insights.speaker: Katie Drummond
insights.so_what: Underwrite AI-in-media investment as a margin story on a shrinking top line, not a growth story — which means adoption accelerates in downturns.
insights.quote: The cost of movies keeps going up, whereas the box office is not necessarily covering that.
insights.locator: If you talk to people at the studios

insights.claim: Pixar originals effectively cannot be made for less than $200 million because of a California-based, labor-intensive proprietary process that has not adopted AI to the extent it could — making it the most exposed cost structure in animation.
insights.speaker: Katie Drummond
insights.so_what: Pixar is the clearest single-asset case for AI-driven cost restructuring inside Disney; watch for pipeline changes or California headcount moves as the tell.
insights.locator: If you look at the animation space

insights.claim: Because the guilds refuse to concede labor cost, the savings must come from the two unprotected sources — non-unionized below-the-line workers and technology — making job displacement a mechanical consequence of the cost math rather than an ideological choice.
insights.speaker: Katie Drummond
insights.so_what: The displacement is concentrated in non-union animation and below-the-line roles; union headline settlements will not signal where the actual employment losses occur.
insights.quote: And the guilds aren't bringing the cost of labor down. The unions are not willing to do that. So where does it come from? It comes from non-unionized labor that is, for the most part, the below-the-line people and the technology.
insights.locator: And the guilds aren't bringing the cost of labor down

insights.claim: Studios frame AI as the latest in a sequence of technology shocks — sound, television, VCR, digital, streaming — that were survivable and ultimately profit-enhancing if managed, and treat cost reduction as a fiduciary obligation to shareholders.
insights.speaker: Katie Drummond
insights.so_what: Expect no voluntary studio restraint on AI adoption; the fiduciary framing means talent pressure can slow but not stop it.
insights.quote: They have a fiduciary responsibility to their shareholders to bring down the cost of movies, and they see it as an evolution.
insights.locator: Now, is it gonna stop them? No.

insights.claim: Ben Affleck's AI company sold to Netflix for $587 million — more, per Belloni, than Affleck has earned from all his movies combined — establishing that AI tooling equity now dwarfs traditional talent compensation in Hollywood.
insights.speaker: Katie Drummond
insights.so_what: Talent is being repriced toward founder-equity outcomes; expect more star-fronted AI startups built explicitly as acquisition targets for streamers seeking legitimacy.
insights.quote: He's gonna make more money on that than he's made on any of his movies put together.
insights.locator: That's a lot of money.

insights.claim: The Netflix-Affleck deal is best read as reputational cover rather than pure technology acquisition — a star's credibility purchases the social license for Netflix to pursue AI that peers would be attacked for.
insights.speaker: Katie Drummond
insights.so_what: Acquisition multiples in creative-AI include a legitimacy premium unrelated to the technology — a distortion that inflates comparable valuations across the sector.
insights.quote: Was this a $600 million press release?
insights.locator: Netflix got a lot of leeway on this

insights.claim: The acquired product's actual function is narrow and defensive — making already-shot footage available to generative AI so filmmakers can extend a scene's periphery or get missing coverage without a costly reshoot — positioned as augmentation rather than replacement.
insights.speaker: Katie Drummond
insights.so_what: Reshoot elimination is the first credible ROI line for generative AI in live action; it targets a real, budgetable cost rather than replacing creative labor.
insights.locator: And if you look at what that product actually does

insights.claim: Capital is flowing in both directions between tech and Hollywood: Google DeepMind put $75 million into A24, Lionsgate took a stake in AI video company Runway, and Netflix bought Affleck's company — driven partly by C-suite fear of being left behind.
insights.speaker: Katie Drummond
insights.so_what: Cross-holdings between AI labs and studios compromise studios as adversaries in the copyright fight — check the cap table before assuming a studio will litigate.
insights.locator: There have been a bunch of deals between tech firms and Hollywood

insights.claim: Brand-dependent studios pay a direct consumer cost for AI association: A24 took a hit with its own fanbase over the Google deal, and the risk is measurable in merchandise demand because A24's business rests on being a brand among people who care about movies.
insights.speaker: Katie Drummond
insights.so_what: For brand-led indies, AI partnerships carry consumer-revenue risk that the majors do not face — a differentiated exposure worth separating in media coverage.
insights.locator: A24 is a brand among people who care about movies

insights.claim: The market is bifurcating into content audiences experience as authored and real versus content they passively consume, and the more social video fills with generative output the larger the market opening for big, verifiably real theatrical films.
insights.speaker: Katie Drummond
insights.so_what: The contrarian trade in media is long premium, verifiably human theatrical product as AI floods the low end — scarcity value rises as production cost falls elsewhere.
insights.quote: There's going to be a split between things that we find authentic and those that we just kind of passively enjoy.
insights.locator: And I say real in the sense that movies

insights.claim: The Odyssey's commercial breakthrough is attributed to perceptible authorship rather than spectacle — audiences can detect when something is authored, and knowing a real shot (dolphins beside the boat) is real is the differentiator studios risk squandering in pursuit of lower costs.
insights.speaker: Katie Drummond
insights.so_what: Verified-real provenance may become a marketable asset class in film; watch for studios formalizing 'shot in camera' claims the way food brands use origin labeling.
insights.quote: it smells authored, and the audience can tell when something is authored
insights.locator: But what I would argue to the studios

insights.claim: The authored-blockbuster model is not replicable at scale — Nolan is described as a one of one who arrived with an Oscar for Oppenheimer and a billion-dollar gross, and The Odyssey made by anyone else would be made for far less than its roughly $250 to $300 million cost without the star cast.
insights.speaker: Katie Drummond
insights.so_what: The authenticity moat depends on a handful of individual filmmakers, making it a key-person risk rather than a durable studio capability.
insights.locator: He is a one of one at this point

insights.claim: Talent relations carry hard financial consequences: Warner Bros. lost Christopher Nolan permanently after putting its entire 2021 slate day-and-date on HBO Max, and Universal captured the number one filmmaker in town as a result.
insights.speaker: Katie Drummond
insights.so_what: A precedent directly applicable to AI: a tech-forward decision that alienates top talent can cost a studio a franchise-scale relationship for a decade.
insights.locator: The whole reason Christopher Nolan made The Odyssey

insights.claim: The risk of over-adoption is losing the differentiator entirely — if a broadcast lineup becomes AI slop, the studios forfeit the one attribute that distinguishes their product from the infinite AI content already saturating social platforms.
insights.speaker: Katie Drummond
insights.so_what: The bear case for media AI is self-inflicted commoditization — cost savings that destroy the pricing power they were meant to protect.
insights.locator: I think it needs to be managed properly

insights.claim: Emerging creators are not uniformly pro-AI: Kane Parsons, whose Backrooms became A24's highest-grossing film, said he would probably make generative AI disappear if he could — and studios care because they are ultimately in the talent-relations business.
insights.speaker: Katie Drummond
insights.so_what: Next-generation hitmakers are a constituency studios must court, which imposes a real ceiling on how openly studios can adopt generative tools.
insights.locator: Then you have someone like Kane Parsons

themes.theme: Guild lines and where they fail

insights.claim: SAG-AFTRA's position is explicitly not anti-AI but anti-displacement, and its mechanism is economic neutralization: using a synthetic performer triggers a fee that makes it just as costly as hiring a human actor.
insights.speaker: Katie Drummond
insights.so_what: Cost-parity clauses, not bans, are how organized labor is defusing AI — a template likely to spread to other creative industries and to blunt the savings thesis for on-camera work.
insights.quote: We are not against the use of AI. We are against the use of AI that causes job loss for our members.
insights.locator: We've seen it come up as an issue in labor negotiations

insights.claim: The Writers Guild permits AI as a drafting aid but requires a credited human writer on every script and bars AI from being the author of a guild-covered script — preserving the credit, and therefore the residual, rather than blocking the tool.
insights.speaker: Katie Drummond
insights.so_what: The protected asset is credit and residual economics, not the work itself — meaning AI can absorb writing labor without touching guild revenue, for now.
insights.locator: You may not know this, but the Writers Guild

insights.claim: The unprotected exposure is below-the-line and animation, where coverage is patchwork across Teamsters and IATSE and many animation jobs are not union-covered at all — those roles are described as the most vulnerable and are already being eliminated.
insights.speaker: Katie Drummond
insights.so_what: Job losses will show up in non-union animation and support roles first, invisible to guild-negotiation headlines — a leading indicator hiding outside the reported data.
insights.locator: That's where it gets to the below-the-line union

insights.claim: Belloni explicitly declines to endorse Jeffrey Katzenberg's claim that 80 to 90 percent of an animated film's workforce will be replaced by AI, saying that will not be the case at least for a while, while conceding elimination is already underway.
insights.speaker: Katie Drummond
insights.so_what: Treat headline displacement percentages from AI-invested executives as promotional; the informed base case is gradual automation, not workforce collapse.
insights.locator: I'm not prepared to go all the way

insights.claim: A gray labor market is emerging in which underemployed Hollywood workers earn money training the AI models that displaced them, though Belloni judges it not yet prevalent while noting a widespread screenwriter fear that their work is being used for training without consent.
insights.speaker: Katie Drummond
insights.so_what: Expert-labeler demand from creative professionals is a real but small emerging market; the larger signal is unconsented training as the industry's dominant grievance.
insights.locator: I wanted to ask you about what some have called an emerging gray market

insights.claim: The legal status quo is that no court has definitively held that using copyrighted material inside a model is itself infringement, so the stronger current theory is that the model's output expression infringes — you can ingest every Disney character, but a result that looks too much like Mickey Mouse is the violation.
insights.speaker: Katie Drummond
insights.so_what: The output-versus-ingestion distinction is the single variable determining whether AI labs face manageable filtering costs or existential training-data liability.
insights.quote: There has not been a definitive determination that using copyrighted material in a model is itself copyright infringement.
insights.locator: So, I have an opinion.

insights.claim: The entertainment industry's strategic objective is to move courts toward ruling that mere ingestion is infringement, but a former entertainment lawyer's read is that the case law is not trending that way.
insights.speaker: Katie Drummond
insights.so_what: The bear case for content owners: litigation may cap output similarity without ever creating a licensing market for training data.
insights.locator: Now, the entertainment industry would very much like

insights.claim: The $1.5 billion authors' settlement with Anthropic — described as the biggest in copyright law history — is read as evidence the defendant either had too-similar output or feared setting precedent on the ingestion question.
insights.speaker: Katie Drummond
insights.so_what: Settlement magnitude establishes a price anchor for training-data liability that will inform every subsequent studio negotiation and any provisioning by AI labs.
insights.locator: But, you know, there was just this settlement in the book case

insights.claim: Disney and Universal's suit against Midjourney, later joined by Warner Bros., has entered a discovery phase in which Midjourney's lawyers are demanding the studios disclose how they already use AI — turning the plaintiffs' own adoption into a defense weapon.
insights.speaker: Katie Drummond
insights.so_what: Discovery exposure is why quietly AI-adopting studios may prefer settlement to precedent; watch for quiet resolutions rather than landmark rulings.
insights.locator: Because Midjourney's lawyers are now demanding

insights.claim: Finished films are largely absent from open-web training corpora — you would have to go to piracy, and no comprehensive screenplay database exists — which distinguishes film IP from text and images in the training-data debate.
insights.speaker: Katie Drummond
insights.so_what: Film and TV may retain more genuine data leverage than publishers did, because the corpus was never freely scraped — a stronger licensing position than the book industry had.
insights.locator: But for the most part, most finished movies are not

insights.claim: Belloni's own position is that fair use was never contemplated to permit scraping the entire internet, and that hundreds of millions of dollars of created IP should be protectable against systems generating competing characters.
insights.speaker: Katie Drummond
insights.so_what: The informed industry-insider view is that the legal outcome is unsettled and the labs are actively exploiting that vagueness — a five-to-ten-year overhang on media IP valuations.
insights.quote: But to use a fair-use exception to scrape the entire internet, which certainly was not contemplated when the copyright laws were first enacted, I think that’s a stretch.
insights.locator: Whether that ultimately wins the day

insights.claim: The core structural conflict is default-setting: tech companies operate on an opt-out, ask-forgiveness model while the entertainment industry wants the default to be exclusion with opt-in consent for name, image and likeness.
insights.speaker: Katie Drummond
insights.so_what: Whichever default wins determines whether likeness becomes a licensable revenue stream for talent or a free input for model builders — the single largest value-transfer question in the sector.
insights.quote: It’s an ask-forgiveness mentality rather than an ask-permission one.
insights.locator: They realized that pissed people off

insights.claim: Two parallel approaches are being pursued: a private consent infrastructure via RSL Media's Human Consent Registry, cofounded by Cate Blanchett and backed by CAA, and a legislative route where SAG-AFTRA seeks a federal right of publicity to replace the current state-law patchwork.
insights.speaker: Katie Drummond
insights.so_what: A federal right of publicity would be the durable outcome since copyright is already federal; the private registry only works with voluntary AI-company buy-in that is not assured.
insights.locator: What about human performers and the idea of voice and likeness?

insights.claim: Talent agencies CAA and WME are meeting individually with AI companies seeking a blanket opt-out covering all their clients, but little is publicly known about the terms of those deals.
insights.speaker: Katie Drummond
insights.so_what: Agencies are positioning as the collective rights clearinghouse for likeness — potentially a new high-margin revenue line if opt-in licensing becomes the norm.
insights.locator: You've also reported on agencies like CAA and WME

insights.claim: Sora's practical value collapsed once copyrighted images were restricted, illustrating that consumer demand for generative video is substantially demand for unauthorized IP mashups rather than for the generation capability itself.
insights.speaker: Katie Drummond
insights.so_what: If engagement depends on infringing content, then compliant generative video products face a much smaller addressable market than launch metrics implied.
insights.locator: Especially when you couldn't use copyrighted images in it

insights.claim: Amazon's ownership of MGM makes it an MPA member, and it refused to sign off on an anti-generative-image statement, which is why the studios' lobbying arm produced no four-alarm response to Sora despite eighty years of anti-piracy advocacy.
insights.speaker: Katie Drummond
insights.so_what: Industry trade bodies are now structurally unable to act against AI because their members are AI buyers — collective-action failure is the sector's defining governance problem.
insights.locator: So, Sora comes along, right?

insights.claim: The three biggest buyers of entertainment content among the top six are Amazon, Netflix and Apple — meaning the majority of demand for Hollywood's output now sits with companies whose primary businesses are technology.
insights.speaker: Katie Drummond
insights.so_what: Content pricing power and editorial independence both flow from buyer concentration; tech buyers have interests that override traditional studio incentives.
insights.quote: The three biggest buyers of entertainment content right now among the top six are Amazon, Netflix, and Apple.
insights.locator: So, it's just a very fraught problem for the industry

insights.claim: Amazon MGM shelved the completed Sam Altman film Artificial after spending $40 million on it, in February — the same period Amazon announced a $50 billion deal with OpenAI — offloading it to Neon for $0 up front against a $15 million theatrical release commitment while eating the remaining cost.
insights.speaker: Katie Drummond
insights.so_what: A quantified price for commercial deference: roughly $25 million written off to avoid antagonizing a $50 billion counterparty — the clearest evidence yet that AI partnerships now govern editorial decisions.
insights.quote: Amazon is essentially eating the rest of the cost with the hope that it will become a big box office hit and they will recoup their money, and they did that to get out of this situation, to not have a problem with Sam Altman.
insights.locator: So Mike Hopkins, the head of Prime Video

insights.claim: Front-end self-censorship is common — studios passed on The Apprentice rather than antagonize Donald Trump, and it earned two Oscar nominations for tiny distributor Briarcliff — but abandoning an already-completed film is described as genuinely rare, with the closest precedent being A&E offloading The Kennedys roughly fifteen years ago.
insights.speaker: Katie Drummond
insights.so_what: Distinguish routine greenlight avoidance from post-completion dumping; the latter signals a counterparty relationship valued above sunk production capital and is a new escalation.
insights.quote: But it's very rare to make a movie and then dump it.
insights.locator: So that's an example where that happened

insights.claim: The test case for whether Hollywood can still criticize tech is Sony's release of The Social Reckoning, Aaron Sorkin's Facebook Files follow-up connecting Meta's engagement decisions to January 6th — notably from the one studio with no streaming service, Japanese ownership, and no Trump settlement.
insights.speaker: Katie Drummond
insights.so_what: Structural independence — no streaming service, foreign ownership, no political settlements — is becoming the prerequisite for adversarial content, a new axis for evaluating media companies.
insights.locator: I mean, we're going to get an answer this fall

insights.claim: Movie virality is now substantially purchased: viral marketers openly claim to pump out hundreds of thousands of positive and negative tweets weekly on a single title, and the default assumption should be that any social post about a major release is paid.
insights.speaker: Katie Drummond
insights.so_what: Social sentiment is unusable as a demand signal for entertainment; any model using social buzz to forecast box office is measuring marketing spend, not audience interest.
insights.quote: If you’re interested in what the new Spider-Man movie is and whether it’s good, and you go on social media, chances are the tweet you see will be paid for.
insights.locator: My rule is: Trust nothing.

insights.claim: What is new is not paid publicity but algorithmic amplification — marketers who know how to game recommendation systems can saturate the feeds of anyone interested in a franchise, in either a positive or negative direction.
insights.speaker: Katie Drummond
insights.so_what: Coordinated negative campaigns are now a real commercial weapon against competitors' titles — an unmodeled risk factor in film revenue forecasts.
insights.locator: But what's different now is that the algorithms

insights.claim: Negative astroturf campaigns can be survived by strong product: an anti-Odyssey troll campaign, encouraged after Elon Musk publicly disliked the film, failed to stop it, though most films cannot overcome such campaigns.
insights.speaker: Katie Drummond
insights.so_what: Only franchise-scale titles with authentic demand can absorb a coordinated attack; mid-tier releases are the vulnerable cohort.
insights.locator: The Odyssey stuff is a perfect example

insights.claim: Rotten Tomatoes has been degraded as a quality signal by its open critic-accreditation process, awards journalists who inflate scores to secure star interviews, PR firms paying critics, and a binary thumbs-up metric that miscounts mostly-negative reviews as positive on the strength of one blurbable line.
insights.speaker: Katie Drummond
insights.so_what: Metacritic's 1-to-100 scale and stricter curation is the recommended surviving signal — a live example of how aggregation platforms lose value once the incentive to game them exceeds the cost.
insights.quote: Rotten Tomatoes is sort of garbage now.
insights.locator: My rule is trust nothing, but that's sort of an easy cop-out

insights.claim: Premiere 'first reactions' are structurally worthless — bloggers and influencers are invited and treated like kings with the expectation of fawning, trade media then aggregates those reactions into a studio-authored narrative, and titles that later bombed had glowing first reactions.
insights.speaker: Katie Drummond
insights.so_what: Discount opening-week sentiment entirely; the manufactured-narrative pipeline runs from paid influencers through trade coverage into critic aggregates, contaminating each layer.
insights.locator: A lot of times you'll see "first reactions"
